procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower criminal court in Uttar Pradesh where the charge-sheet was filed and criminal proceedings were initiated.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 23rd May, 2022 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad dismissing an application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed an application under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr. PC) in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad on 5th October, 2018, seeking to quash the charge-sheet and the pending criminal proceedings against him. The High Court dismissed this application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the charge-sheet, initially approached the High Court. After the High Court dismissed his application, he appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, questioning the High Court's judgment and order. The appellant argued that the High Court failed to consider the facts and circumstances of the proceedings including the charge-sheet in the proper perspective and occasioned a grave failure of justice in rejecting such challenge. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court is set aside.
Criminal Case No.376 of 2016 is quashed.
Parties shall bear their own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellant's application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the criminal proceedings.

facts: The appellant filed an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) before the High Court, seeking to quash a charge-sheet and the resulting criminal proceedings.
The appellant argued that the proceedings were initiated with malicious intent for harassment and to interfere with a pending civil dispute.
The High Court dismissed the application, reasoning that its jurisdiction under Section 482 is limited and it cannot appreciate evidence at this stage to determine if a prima facie case exists.
law: The jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. allows a High Court to quash criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the process of law or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
While this power should be exercised sparingly and with caution, it can be invoked when allowing proceedings to continue would be an abuse of the legal process.
application: The High Court applied the principle of limited jurisdiction, stating that since the allegations were factual and required evidence, it could not conclude that no cognizable offence was disclosed.
The Supreme Court, however, took a different view. It examined the circumstances of the case and found that the criminal proceedings were indeed an abuse of the process of law.
The Supreme Court determined that despite the High Court's reluctance to weigh evidence, the facts of this particular case warranted intervention to prevent injustice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was incorrect in dismissing the application. It held that allowing the criminal case to continue would be an abuse of the process of law. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the essential ingredient for an offence under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act, that the alleged caste-related abuses were uttered 'in any place within public view', was satisfied.

facts: The prosecution intended to rely on the evidence of only three witnesses: the complainant, his wife, and their son.
Neither the First Information Report (FIR) nor the charge sheet mentioned the presence of any other individual, specifically a member of the public, at the place of the incident.
The incident likely took place at the house of the appellant.
law: An essential ingredient for an offence under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act is that the alleged caste-related abuses must be uttered 'in any place within public view'.
application: The court examined the FIR and the charge sheet to determine who was present during the altercation.
It found that the only individuals present were the appellant, the complainant, and the complainant's immediate family (wife and son).
The court reasoned that since no member of the public was present to witness the alleged utterances, the incident did not occur 'in any place within public view'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the basic ingredient for attracting Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act was missing because the alleged abuses were not made in a place 'within public view', as no member of the public was present at the time of the incident.

issue.issue_text: Whether allowing the criminal proceedings for offences under Sections 323 and 504 of the IPC to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of law.

facts: The appellant was accused of beating the complainant, allegedly causing multiple injuries (Section 323 IPC), and intentionally insulting him (Section 504 IPC).
The charge sheet did not refer to any eyewitnesses other than the complainant's wife and son.
Crucially, there was no medical report to support the complainant's claim of having sustained injuries. Neither the FIR nor the charge sheet specified the nature of the alleged hurt.
The State's counter-affidavit only made a "bald statement" that the complainant sustained injuries without providing any material evidence.
In contrast, the appellant had his own injuries treated immediately after the incident.
The police investigation was completed in a single day, which the court found did "more disservice than service to the cause of justice."
law: To sustain a charge of voluntarily causing hurt under Section 323 IPC, there should be credible evidence supporting the allegation of injury.

A conviction under Section 504 IPC is not warranted by the mere fact that the accused abused the complainant; there must be an act amounting to an intentional insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace.
Criminal proceedings can be quashed to prevent an abuse of the process of law, especially when the prosecution's case lacks a "ring of truth."
application: The Court found the prosecution's case regarding the Section 323 charge to be entirely unsubstantiated. The absence of a medical report to corroborate the complainant's alleged injuries was a critical failure.
The Court noted that if the complainant's version were true, the Investigating Officer should have obtained a medical report.

The Court contrasted the lack of evidence for the complainant's injuries with the fact that the appellant himself sought medical treatment for his injuries, which weakened the prosecution's narrative.
Due to the glaring lack of evidence and the shoddy one-day investigation, the Court found "no ring of truth in the prosecution case" for either the Section 323 or the Section 504 charge.
The Court held that the High Court had "misdirected itself" and caused a "grave failure of justice" by refusing to quash the proceedings, as the deficiencies in the prosecution's case were apparent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that allowing the criminal proceedings under Sections 323 and 504 IPC to continue would be an abuse of the process of law. This was because the prosecution's case lacked any credible evidence, particularly a medical report to support the alleged injuries, and the investigation was deeply flawed. Finding no "ring of truth" in the allegations, the Court quashed the criminal case.

cases.case_name: Fiona Shrikhande and Anr. v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The jurisdiction under Section 482, Cr. PC should be sparingly exercised with complete circumspection and caution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The legal principles articulated in paragraphs 15 and 16 of the decision in Hitesh Verma v. The State of Uttarakhand and Anr. can be applied to support the quashing of criminal proceedings.
obiter: It is settled law that the jurisdiction under Section 482, Cr. PC should be sparingly exercised with complete circumspection and caution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court misdirected itself in failing to appreciate the challenge to the criminal proceedings in the proper perspective, which occasioned a grave failure of justice. It would be an abuse of the process of law to allow the criminal case to continue because, even if the appellant abused the complainant, the abuse by itself did not meet the criminal threshold, as it clearly lacked the ingredient of an intentional insult of such a degree that it could provoke a person to break public peace or commit any other offence.
legal_tests_applied: If the contents of the F.I.R., taken on their face value, does not make out any case against the appellant, such an F.I.R. registered with ulterior motive deserves to be quashed.

To warrant subjecting an accused to trial, there must be the presence of the ingredient of intentional insult of such a degree that it could provoke a person to break public peace or commit any other offence.
The jurisdiction under Section 482, Cr. PC should be exercised to prevent an abuse of the process of law and to correct a grave failure of justice.
policy_considerations: It would be an abuse of the process of law to allow continuation of Criminal Case No.376 of 2016.
The High Court... occasioned a grave failure of justice in rejecting such challenge.
